records.sourceFile: Why Exercise may be Beneficial in    Concussion Rehabilitation- A Cellular Perspective.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology (ion dysregulation, energy crisis, impaired neurovascular coupling) and of cellular signalling pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) that mild exercise may influence after concussion. The authors argue that mild, sub-symptom exercise introduced early may support recovery, while noting that higher intensity may be harmful. They cite human studies in which absolute rest was not better than usual care with progressive activity, and note that several human studies infer autonomic dysfunction from proxy measures.
records.limitations: No systematic search is described, and the cellular argument is largely theoretical, supported by mouse data and indirect human measures rather than measured human cellular responses. The exercise dose estimates it cites come from other sources and are not tested here.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the mechanistic pathways as proof that early exercise speeds concussion recovery, when the review presents these links as theoretical and the dose as needing individual judgement.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review of 32 randomised controlled trials of mindfulness-based interventions in athletes (1,788 athletes in total, mean age 23.7 years, across many sports and levels), searched in five databases with no date limit. Seven trials were reported in the abstract as meta-analysed, but the results report pooled analyses of 3 trials (mindfulness; SMD 0.50, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.83), 5 trials (mindfulness-related psychological components; SMD 0.81, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.10) and 4 trials (mental health; SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.29, not significant). Performance was synthesised narratively, with the authors reporting that all included studies showed improvement.
records.limitations: Each pooled analysis rests on only 3 to 5 trials, with high heterogeneity (I2 up to 89 percent), so the estimates are fragile. The paper's own study counts conflict (seven in the abstract, nineteen quantitatively analysed in the discussion), and 6 of 32 trials were rated high risk of bias.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the pooled effects as evidence that mindfulness training improves athletic performance, when performance was only summarised narratively across varied measures and the quantitative results are for mindfulness and psychological factors.
